extracted.intended_audience: education researchers and journalism/ composition educators
extracted.subtask_description: A survey-based comparative study of journalism students at two institutions asking how well freshman composition and introductory journalism courses taught specific writing skills and how useful students found composition for academic/work/journalistic writing; includes analyses of predictors of course success (A grades) using correlations and Cramer's V.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of freshman composition writing instruction (Question 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: How valuable was the writing instruction you received in your first freshman English composition course? (response categories summarized as 'quite a bit' or 'very much')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported percentages and means (SMSU 44.5%, SDSU 46.9%, TOTAL 45.5%; mean TOTAL 3.38, SD 1.04). Chi-square tests by subgroup generally not significant. Authors interpret overall that only composition grade (.186) was a good predictor for this question across institutions. Use as an outcome measure of perceived value of composition for students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness of English composition for the work world (Question 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: How useful for the work world was the writing instruction you received in your first freshman composition course? ('quite a bit' or 'very much')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported percentages and means (SMSU 35.6%, SDSU 21.9%, TOTAL 29.9%; mean TOTAL 2.99, SD 0.99). Chi-square tests not significant overall. Authors note English ACT was the best predictor for this question in some analyses; overall English ACT (.118) was the only good predictor for Question 2 in summary analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of freshman composition for other academic writing (Question 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: How useful for your other academic writing (other than journalism) was the writing instruction you received in freshman composition? ('quite a bit' or 'very much')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported percentages and means (SMSU 46.7%, SDSU 46.9%, TOTAL 46.8%; mean TOTAL 3.30, SD 1.02). Composition grade was the best predictor for this question (composition grade .163 overall), followed closely by journalism grade (.156).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of freshman composition for journalistic writing (Question 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: How useful for your journalistic writing was the writing instruction you received in your first freshman composition course? ('quite a bit' or 'very much')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported percentages and means (SMSU 26.7%, SDSU 18.8%, TOTAL 23.4%; mean TOTAL 2.69, SD 1.00). Overall English ACT (.138) was reported as the only good predictor for Question 4 in summary analyses; responses indicate students typically saw composition as less useful for journalistic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of grammar instruction in freshman composition (Question 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' report of how much grammar instruction they received in their first freshman composition course ('quite a bit' or 'very much')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A minority reported a high amount (SMSU 17.8%, SDSU 21.9%, TOTAL 19.5%; mean TOTAL 2.67, SD 1.04). Authors discuss this relative to perceptions of grammar emphasis and later analyses of correlations with grades (no consistent strong predictive relationship overall).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of grammar instruction in high school English (Question 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' report of how much grammar instruction they received in high school English classes (10th–12th grades)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large majority reported a high amount (SMSU 64.4%, SDSU 65.6%, TOTAL 64.9%; mean TOTAL 3.88, SD 0.99). Used as a variable in correlation analyses with college course grades; authors note no statistically significant correlations overall between high school grammar amount and college grades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor strictness grading for grammar in freshman composition (Question 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Student perception of how strict the freshman composition instructor was in grading for grammar mistakes ('quite a bit' or 'very much')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximately a minority reported the instructor was quite strict (SMSU 46.7%, SDSU 46.9%, TOTAL 46.8%; mean TOTAL 3.30, SD 1.02). Authors report no consistent significant correlation between this strictness measure and college course grades overall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor strictness grading for spelling in freshman composition (Question 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Student perception of how strict the freshman composition instructor was in grading for spelling mistakes ('quite a bit' or 'very much')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A majority reported the instructor was quite strict on spelling (SMSU 62.2%, SDSU 65.6%, TOTAL 64.6%; mean TOTAL 3.73? noted in tables). Authors interpret spelling as seen by students to be a worse error than grammar in freshman composition; no consistent predictive relationship with course outcomes reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: How well students liked their freshman composition course (Question 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' liking of their first freshman composition course ('quite a bit' or 'very much')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported percentages and means (SMSU 62.2%, SDSU 46.9%, TOTAL 55.8%; mean TOTAL 3.60, SD 1.23). Institutional differences are notable (SMSU higher liking); used to contextualize perceptions of usefulness and instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: How well students liked the writing portions of their introductory journalism course (Question 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' liking of the writing portions of their introductory journalism writing courses ('quite a bit' or 'very much')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported percentages and means (SMSU 70.5%, SDSU 40.6%, TOTAL 57.9%; mean TOTAL 3.75, SD 0.80). Large institutional differences; authors use this to compare enthusiasm for journalism vs composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of time devoted to writing in freshman composition vs literature (Question 11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' view of amount of time devoted to writing in freshman composition compared to literature ('not enough' vs other responses)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported 'not enough' percentages (SMSU 20.0%, SDSU 31.3%, TOTAL 24.7%). Used to assess whether students felt composition spent adequate time on writing relative to literature; authors note a minority thought not enough time was devoted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of time devoted to writing in introductory journalism course vs non-writing topics (Question 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students' view of amount of time devoted to writing in the introductory journalism writing course compared to time spent on non-writing topics ('not enough')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Not enough' responses were low (SMSU 11.4%, SDSU 12.5%, TOTAL 11.9%). Authors interpret students were less likely to state insufficient time for writing in journalism courses than in composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concisely (one of the 11 writing skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rated how well freshman composition and introductory journalism taught ability to write concisely (one of 11 skills students evaluated)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall journalism mean was substantially higher than composition (+1.12 overall). In SMSU and SDSU journalism rated higher for conciseness; used in rankings and Pearson r/Spearman rho comparisons showing differences between course emphases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precisely (one of the 11 writing skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rated how well courses taught ability to write precisely
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall journalism mean higher (+0.96 overall). Journalism tended to be rated higher than composition for precision across institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly (one of the 11 writing skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rated how well courses taught ability to write clearly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall journalism mean higher (+0.77 overall). Journalism rated higher on clarity; included in the top practical skills journalism students associated with their journalism courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized (one of the 11 writing skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rated how well courses taught organized writing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism mean higher overall (+0.55). 'Organized' was among the highest-rated skills in both composition and journalism at one or both institutions; listed among similarities (writing for the audience, writing concisely, organized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar (one of the 11 writing skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rated how well courses taught correct grammar
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall journalism mean higher (+0.55 overall), but institutional patterns varied (e.g., SDSU composition rated highly for grammar). Noted by authors as one of the skills where courses differed most in some comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling (one of the 11 writing skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rated how well courses taught correct spelling
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall journalism mean higher (+0.63 overall). Spelling cited as a weakness in freshman composition by students and a skill with large differences between courses/institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience (one of the 11 writing skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rated how well courses taught writing for an audience
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall journalism mean higher (+0.61 overall). Writing for the audience was identified as the skill taught most similarly between composition and journalism and was high in rankings for both courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interestingly (writing interestingly) (one of the 11 skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rated how well courses taught writing interestingly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall small positive difference for journalism (+0.05 overall). Composition students reported some differences; 'writing interestingly' appeared among skills where courses were similar in some comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creatively (writing creatively) (one of the 11 skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rated how well courses taught creative writing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall composition mean was higher (difference -0.47 overall indicates composition > journalism). Authors note composition was more associated with creative and opinionated writing, while journalism emphasized practical skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: In detail (writing in detail) (one of the 11 skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rated how well courses taught writing in detail
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall small positive difference for journalism (+0.13 overall). Composition sometimes rated higher on this skill at some institutions; but overall journalism slightly higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinions (using one's opinions) (one of the 11 skills)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rated how well courses taught use of opinions in writing
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overall composition mean was higher (difference -0.89 overall indicates composition > journalism). Authors interpret that composition emphasizes reflective/opinionated writing while journalism emphasizes practical/objective skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success in introductory journalism course (receiving an A) — outcome and predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving an A in the introductory journalistic writing course as a measured outcome and analyses of variables that predict that success
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a dependent variable in chi-square, Cramer's V, and correlation analyses. Overall the best predictors of an A in journalism were composite ACT (.461 overall), English ACT (.407), sex (.371), composition grade (.132), and major (.111). Institution differences: at SDSU English ACT (.566) and composite ACT/other values were stronger; at SMSU composite ACT (.4251) and English ACT (.3441) were significant predictors. Authors discuss that ACT scores were generally better predictors than composition grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiving an A in freshman composition — outcome and predictors
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving an A in freshman composition as a dependent variable and analyses of variables predicting that outcome
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composite ACT was the best predictor of composition grade overall (.320), followed by English ACT (.270), journalism grade (.132), and major (.123). Institutional differences: at SDSU composite ACT (.583) was a particularly strong predictor. Used to assess how prior achievement predicts course outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cramer's V threshold and use (.100 threshold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of Cramer's V as a normed measure of association and the chosen threshold for interpreting 'high' vs 'low' association
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of small sample size, authors selected a V score of .100 as the dividing point between 'high' and 'low' scores for the sample (about half scores above and below .100). Cramer's V values over .100 were defined as the best predictors in tables summarizing associations between independent variables and dependent survey/question outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Pearson r and Spearman rho to compare course ratings
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical approach for assessing similarity of mean ratings and ranked orderings across courses and institutions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pearson r correlations were calculated based on means to compare how similarly the 11 skills were rated for composition vs journalism; Spearman rho correlations were calculated based on rankings. Examples reported: SMSU comp/jrn Pearson r = -0.266, SDSU comp/jrn r = .035, SMSU comp/SDSU comp r = .668 (significant), SMSU jrn/SDSU jrn r = .955 (highly significant). Authors use these to conclude courses emphasize different skills and to quantify inter-institution similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course emphasis: practical (journalism) vs reflective (composition) skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretive criterion comparing the overall emphasis of freshman composition versus introductory journalism on practical vs reflective writing skills
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors conclude the two courses emphasize different skills: journalism students reported journalism taught practical skills (concise, precise, clear, organized, grammar, spelling, audience) while composition taught more reflective/creative skills (writing interestingly, in detail, using opinions, creativity). This interpretive rubric is supported by the 11-skill ratings and correlation analyses.
